text: Rachel Kerry O'Reilly MBE FRS FRSC is a British chemist and Professor at the University of Birmingham. She specializes at the intersection of biology and materials, developing polymers that mimic natural nanomaterials like viruses and cells. She is a Fellow of both the Royal Society of Chemistry and the Royal Society. O'Reilly was born in Holywood and attended a grammar school; she has dyslexia. She studied Natural Sciences at the University of Cambridge, working with Brian F. G. Johnson on her Master's project, and graduated in 1999. She then moved to Imperial College London to work with Vernon C. Gibson on catalyst design, earning a PhD in 2003. O'Reilly joined Craig Hawker and Karen L. Wooley at Washington University in St. Louis, where she demonstrated the fabrication of cross-linked polymer nanoparticles that were Click-ready. In 2004, she was awarded a Royal Commission for the Exhibition of 1851 fellowship, and took up a research fellowship at Downing College, Cambridge in 2005. At Cambridge, she received a Royal Society Dorothy Hodgkin fellowship and developed hollow polymeric nanocages capable of selectively recognising substrates. She joined the University of Warwick in 2009 as an Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council career-acceleration fellow, focusing on water-soluble responsive polymer scaffolds with catalytic domains and responsive polymers that could trigger the release of catalysts into surrounding media. She was appointed Professor in 2012 at the age of 34. That year, she became the first UK winner of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry Samsung Young Polymer Scientist prize. In 2012, she appeared on Start the Week with Andrew Marr, where he described her as "a chemist who does strange things with plastics". In 2013, she received the American Chemical Society Hermann Mark Young Scholar award. She was appointed Professor of Chemistry at the University of Birmingham in 2017. In addition to her research, O'Reilly is an enthusiastic geologist and enjoys travelling to volcanoes. She was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry in 2013 and named one of the Royal Society of Chemistry's 175 Faces of Chemistry. In 2023, she was elected an Honorary Fellow of Downing College, Cambridge.
